items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a farm viewed as a system with inputs (land, labour, capital, seeds), processes (ploughing, harvesting) and outputs (crops, livestock, income)”.
items.answer: Agricultural system
items.markingKey: Agricultural system: a farm viewed as a system with inputs (land, labour, capital, seeds), processes (ploughing, harvesting) and outputs (crops, livestock, income). [1]

items.stem: Explain the physical factors affecting agricultural land use.
items.answer: Temperature and growing season, rainfall and its reliability, relief and slope, altitude, soil type, depth and drainage, aspect, risk of frost, drought and flood.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor with effect [4]

items.stem: Explain the human factors affecting agricultural land use.
items.answer: Markets and transport, capital and technology, labour supply, land tenure and farm size, government policy (subsidies, quotas), culture and diet, knowledge.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor [4]

items.stem: Table 17.1 shows data for three farms: area (ha), number of workers and output (tonnes per hectare per year). wet rice farm, Bangladesh: 0.9 ha, 5 workers, 6.3 t/ha of rice; wheat farm, Saskatchewan, Canada: 1 210 ha, 4 workers, 2.6 t/ha of wheat; cattle ranch, Queensland, Australia: 57 935 ha, 6 workers, 0.0051 t/ha of beef (liveweight). Explain why output per hectare is so low on the cattle ranch.
items.answer: Semi-arid climate with low, unreliable rainfall gives sparse pasture, so stocking density must be very low; long distances to markets; low inputs.

items.stem: Table 17.1 shows data for three farms: area (ha), number of workers and output (tonnes per hectare per year). wet rice farm, Bangladesh: 1.3 ha, 4 workers, 5.4 t/ha of rice; wheat farm, Saskatchewan, Canada: 920 ha, 4 workers, 2.6 t/ha of wheat; cattle ranch, Queensland, Australia: 58 540 ha, 8 workers, 0.0028 t/ha of beef (liveweight). (a) Explain why output per hectare is so low on the cattle ranch. (b) Explain why the rice farm uses so much labour.
items.answer: (a) Semi-arid climate with low, unreliable rainfall gives sparse pasture, so stocking density must be very low; long distances to markets; low inputs. (b) Small plots, terracing, transplanting, weeding and water control are done by hand; labour is plentiful and cheap; capital for machinery is scarce.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that physical factors are less important than human factors in explaining agricultural land use. In your answer you may refer to policy, technology and markets.
items.answer: For: Markets, capital, technology, government policy and land tenure explain much land use, especially in HICs (Dutch horticulture, irrigation in deserts). Against: Climate, soil and relief set the limits for crops and livestock (e.g. rice needs warmth and water; ranching in semi-arid areas); physical risk remains important in LICs. Conclusion: Physical factors set the possible range of land uses, while human factors decide which are actually chosen; human factors grow in importance with development.

items.stem: Compare intensive and extensive farming systems.
items.answer: Intensive: small areas, high inputs of labour or capital, high yields per ha (rice in Bangladesh, Dutch greenhouses). Extensive: large areas, low inputs per ha, low yields per ha but often high output per worker (Australian ranches, Canadian wheat).

items.stem: Explain the factors that cause food insecurity.
items.answer: Physical: drought, floods, pests, soil degradation. Human: poverty, conflict, high food prices, poor infrastructure and storage, population growth, dependence on imports, poor governance.

items.stem: Explain why a country may produce enough food but still have food insecurity.
items.answer: Poor people cannot afford food; unequal distribution between regions and groups; exports of crops; waste and poor storage; conflict blocking access.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the spread from the 1960s of high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, with fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation, especially in Asia and Latin America”.
items.answer: Green Revolution
items.markingKey: Green Revolution: the spread from the 1960s of high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, with fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation, especially in Asia and Latin America. [1]

items.stem: Explain the positive impacts of the Green Revolution.
items.answer: Yields of wheat and rice doubled or tripled; India became self-sufficient in grain; fewer famines; double cropping; higher incomes for larger farmers; lower food prices.

items.stem: Explain the negative impacts of the Green Revolution.
items.answer: Wider inequality as richer farmers could afford inputs; debt; falling water tables and salinisation (Punjab); pesticide pollution and health effects; loss of crop diversity; mechanisation reducing jobs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per impact [4]

items.stem: Fig. 17.3 shows mean wheat yields in India (tonnes per hectare): 1961: 0.85, 1970: 1.21, 1980: 1.44, 1990: 2.12, 2000: 2.78, 2010: 2.84, 2020: 3.43. Explain one environmental problem caused by the Green Revolution in Punjab.
items.answer: Over-pumping of groundwater for irrigation has lowered water tables by about 0.5-1 m a year in places; or heavy fertiliser and pesticide use pollutes water and soils.

items.stem: Fig. 17.3 shows mean wheat yields in India (tonnes per hectare): 1961: 0.85, 1970: 1.21, 1980: 1.44, 1990: 2.12, 2000: 2.78, 2010: 2.84, 2020: 3.43. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in yield between 1961 and 2010. (b) Calculate the mean annual growth rate of yield between 1961 and 2010.
To what extent do you agree that the benefits of the Green Revolution have outweighed its costs?
items.answer: For: Huge increases in yields and output saved millions from famine; India and other Asian countries became self-sufficient; food prices fell. Against: Environmental damage (groundwater depletion, salinisation, pesticides), rising inequality and debt, loss of biodiversity, farmer distress in Punjab; less success in Africa. Conclusion: Overall the benefits in food supply were huge, but the environmental and social costs mean the model now needs to become more sustainable.

items.stem: Explain why the Green Revolution spread unevenly.
items.answer: HYVs needed irrigation, fertiliser and credit, so areas with water and wealthier farmers adopted first; staple crops of drylands and Africa were neglected; infrastructure and markets varied.

items.answer: (a) Semi-arid climate with low, unreliable rainfall gives sparse pasture, so stocking density must be very low; long distances to markets; low inputs. (b) Small plots, terracing, transplanting, weeding and water control are done by hand; labour is plentiful and cheap; capital for machinery is scarce.

items.stem: “Physical factors are less important than human factors in explaining agricultural land use.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to markets, technology and policy.
items.answer: For: Markets, capital, technology, government policy and land tenure explain much land use, especially in HICs (Dutch horticulture, irrigation in deserts). Against: Climate, soil and relief set the limits for crops and livestock (e.g. rice needs warmth and water; ranching in semi-arid areas); physical risk remains important in LICs. Conclusion: Physical factors set the possible range of land uses, while human factors decide which are actually chosen; human factors grow in importance with development.

items.answer: (a) Correct. Price spikes and supply shocks quickly affect import-dependent countries. (b) Highest in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, linked to poverty, conflict, climate hazards and rapid population growth; low in HICs with high incomes and imports.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “high-yielding variety (HYV)”?
options: A crop variety bred to give much larger yields, often short-stemmed and responsive to fertiliser, such as IR8 rice.
Increasing output per hectare through greater inputs of labour, capital, fertiliser or technology.
The use of genetically modified crops to raise yields or resistance to pests and drought.
Replacing human and animal labour with machines such as tractors and combine harvesters.

items.stem: A revision website states: “The Green Revolution increased the yields of all crops equally.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Wheat and rice gained most; pulses and millets much less.

items.answer: (a) Yields of wheat and rice doubled or tripled; India became self-sufficient in grain; fewer famines; double cropping; higher incomes for larger farmers; lower food prices. (b) Not correct. Production rose greatly, but many people remain undernourished because of poverty.

items.stem: Assess the view that the benefits of the Green Revolution have outweighed its costs.
items.answer: For: Huge increases in yields and output saved millions from famine; India and other Asian countries became self-sufficient; food prices fell. Against: Environmental damage (groundwater depletion, salinisation, pesticides), rising inequality and debt, loss of biodiversity, farmer distress in Punjab; less success in Africa. Conclusion: Overall the benefits in food supply were huge, but the environmental and social costs mean the model now needs to become more sustainable.
